title: حِكَايَةُ الْمَلِكِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ
part: Night 143 · King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 692–702 (Night 143, continuing directly from nights-142), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 143 continues the tale of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān. Bākūn finishes her story of the ruined man in the bath-house, who swallows hashish and dreams he is a great lord bathed, perfumed and attended, until the bathers wake him, laughing, on the cold floor; she talks Kān Mā Kān to sleep and draws her dagger, but his mother, warned by Qaḍā Fakān, comes in time, and Bākūn slips away. Kān Mā Kān leaves the city for the vizier Dandān, Nuzhat al-Zamān follows, and the narrator passes in a few lines over their campaign against the Rūm and their capture by King Rūmzān. Rūmzān dreams of a golden girdle that becomes two and is about to behead his captives when his nurse Marjāna reveals his birth: he is the son of Queen Abrīza and King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, and so Nuzhat al-Zamān's brother and Kān Mā Kān's uncle. The matching beads prove it; the armies are reconciled, al-Zabalkān is given Damascus, the kings march on Iraq vowing vengeance on Dhāt al-Dawāhī, and at Baghdad Rūmzān and Kān Mā Kān agree, on Dandān's counsel, to rule on alternate days. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الثَّالِثَةُ وَالأَرْبَعُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-thālithatu wa-al-arbaʿūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the third-and-forty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and forty-third night,

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّهُ جَلَسَ عَلَى الْفَسْقِيَّةِ وَمَا زَالَ يَنْزَحُ الْمَاءَ عَلَى رَأْسِهِ إِلَى أَنْ تَعِبَ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu annahu jalasa ʿalā al-fasqiyyati wa-mā zāla yanzaḥu al-māʾa ʿalā raʾsihi ilā an taʿiba
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that he sat at the fountain-basin and did not cease drawing the water onto his head until he tired.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the man sat down by the basin and kept pouring water over his head until he was weary.
sentences.n: The print has السعيدا, a misprint for السعيد, corrected here; and النسقية, a misprint for الفسقية, corrected here. As often, the new night opens by repeating the last words of the old one: “he” is the ruined man of Bākūn's story, last seen at the basin of the bath. fasqiyya, “fountain basin”, a post-classical word.

sentences.t: فَخَرَجَ إِلَى الْحَوْضِ الْبَارِدِ فَلَمْ يَجِدْأَ حَدًا فَاخْتَلَى بِنَفْسِهِ وَطَلَّعَ قِطْعَةَ حَشِيشٍ وَبَلَعَهَا فَسَاحَتْ فِي مُخِّهِ فَانْقَلَبَ عَلَى الرُّخَامِ
sentences.tr: fa-kharaja ilā al-ḥawḍi al-bāridi fa-lam yajid aḥadan fa-ikhtalā bi-nafsihi wa-ṭallaʿa qiṭʿata ḥashīshin wa-balaʿahā fa-sāḥat fī mukhkhihi fa-inqalaba ʿalā al-rukhāmi
sentences.l: Then he went-out to the cold pool, and did not find anyone; so he went-apart by himself, and brought-out a piece of hashish and swallowed it; and it melted into his brain, and he toppled over onto the marble.
sentences.i: Then he went out to the cold pool and found no one there. So, alone with himself, he took out a lump of hashish and swallowed it. It melted into his brain, and he rolled over onto the marble.
sentences.n: The print has ني, a misprint for في, corrected here (the word stands at the head of a new line, after فساحت). The print also splits aḥadan, “anyone”, after its first letter, writing يجدا حدا; the spacing is kept and the words are pointed as lam yajid aḥadan. ikhtalā bi-nafsihi, “to be alone with oneself, withdraw”. ṭallaʿa, “to bring out, take out”, is colloquial (Classical akhraja). sāḥat, “it melted, ran”: the feminine agrees with qiṭʿa, the piece of hashish.

sentences.t: وَخَيَّلَ لَهُ الْحَشِيشُ أَنَّ مَهْتَارًا كَبِيرًا يَكْبِسُهُ وَعَبْدَيْنِ وَاقِفَانِ عَلَى رَأْسِهِ وَاحِدٌ مَعَهُ الطَّاسَةُ وَالآخَرُ مَعَهُ آلَةُ الْحَمَّامِ وَمَا يَحْتَاجُ إِلَيْهِ الْبَلَّانُ
sentences.tr: wa-khayyala lahu al-ḥashīshu anna mahtāran kabīran yakbisuhu wa-ʿabdayni wāqifāni ʿalā raʾsihi wāḥidun maʿahu al-ṭāsatu wa-al-ākharu maʿahu ālatu al-ḥammāmi wa-mā yaḥtāju ilayhi al-ballānu
sentences.l: And the hashish made-him-fancy that a great chief-attendant was kneading him, and two slaves standing at his head, one with him the bowl and the other with him the bath-gear and what the bath-man needs.
sentences.i: And the hashish made him fancy that a great head attendant was massaging him, with two slaves standing over him, one holding the bowl and the other the bath things and all that a bath attendant needs.
sentences.n: khayyala lahu, “made him imagine”: the hashish is the subject. mahtār (from Persian mihtar, “chief”) is a head servant or master of a household's attendants. kabasa, “to knead, massage”, is the word for the massage given in the bath; the ballān is the bath attendant who gives it. ʿabdayni wāqifāni: the first word is accusative after anna, the second nominative, a mismatch typical of Middle Arabic. ṭāsa, a shallow metal bowl for pouring water.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَى ذَلِكَ قَالَ فِي نَفْسِهِ كَأَنَّ هَؤُلَاءِ غَلِطُوا فِيَّ أَوْ مِنْ طَائِفَتِنَا الْحَشَّاشِينَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾā dhālika qāla fī nafsihi ka-anna hāʾulāʾi ghaliṭū fiyya aw min ṭāʾifatinā al-ḥashshāshīna
sentences.l: And when he saw that, he said in himself: It-seems these have erred about-me, or (they are) of our band, the hashish-eaters.
sentences.i: When he saw this he said to himself, “These people must have mistaken me for someone else, or else they are of our own fraternity, the hashish-eaters.”
sentences.n: ka-anna, “as though”, used colloquially as “it seems that, surely”; the shadda on كانّ and on فيّ is the print's. ghaliṭa fī, “to mistake (someone)”. ḥashshāsh, “hashish-eater”, an intensive form, here in the regular genitive -īna, in apposition to ṭāʾifatinā, “our band”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُ مَدَّ رِجْلَيْهِ فَتَخَيَّلَ لَهُ أَنَّ الْبَلَّانَ قَالَ لَهُ يَا سَيِّدِى قَدْ أَزِفَ الْوَقْتُ عَلَى طُلُوعِكَ وَالْيَوْمَ نَوْبَتُكَ
sentences.tr: thumma innahu madda rijlayhi fa-takhayyala lahu anna al-ballāna qāla lahu yā sayyidī qad azifa al-waqtu ʿalā ṭulūʿika wa-al-yawma nawbatuka
sentences.l: Then he stretched his legs, and it was-fancied to him that the bath-man said to him: O my master, the time has drawn-near for your going-up, and today is your turn.
sentences.i: Then he stretched out his legs, and fancied that the bath attendant said to him, “My lord, the time for you to go up is close at hand, and today it is your turn.”
sentences.n: thumma innahu, “then he”, a stock narrative link. takhayyala lahu, impersonal, “it seemed to him”. azifa, “to draw near, be imminent”. ṭulūʿ, “going up”: either leaving the bath or, as the attendants' later words suggest, going up to the court to serve, for nawba is a turn of duty. The text does not settle which.

sentences.t: فَضَحِكَ وَقَالَ فِي نَفْسِهِ مَا شَاءَ اللَّهُ يَا حَشِيشُ
sentences.tr: fa-ḍaḥika wa-qāla fī nafsihi mā shāʾa Allāhu yā ḥashīshu
sentences.l: And he laughed and said in himself: What God willed, O hashish!
sentences.i: He laughed and said to himself, “Well done, hashish, God be praised!”
sentences.n: mā shāʾa Allāh, “what God has willed”, the stock exclamation of admiration at something wonderful (and against the evil eye); here he congratulates the drug on its work.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ فَعَلَ وَهُوَ سَاكِتٌ فَقَامَ الْبَلَّانُ وَأَخَذَ بِيَدِهِ وَأَدَارَ عَلَي وَسَطِهِ مِيزَرًا مِنَ الْحَرِيرِ الأَسْوَدِ وَمَشَى الْعَبْدَانِ وَرَاءَهُ بِالطَّاسَاتِ وَالْحَوَائِجِ
sentences.tr: thumma faʿala wa-huwa sākitun fa-qāma al-ballānu wa-akhadha bi-yadihi wa-adāra ʿalā wasaṭihi mīzaran mina al-ḥarīri al-aswadi wa-mashā al-ʿabdāni warāʾahu bi-al-ṭāsāti wa-al-ḥawāʾiji
sentences.l: Then he did (so), and he silent; and the bath-man rose and took him by his hand and wound about his middle a waist-wrap of the black silk, and the two-slaves walked behind him with the bowls and the things.
sentences.i: So he went along with it and kept silent. The attendant got up, took him by the hand and wrapped a waist-cloth of black silk around his middle, and the two slaves walked behind him with the bowls and the rest of the gear.
sentences.n: thumma faʿala, “then he did”, with no object: he did as he was bidden. The phrase is abrupt and may be defective, but it reads. akhadha bi-yadihi, “took him by the hand”: the verb takes bi- for what is grasped. mīzar, the bath wrap worn round the waist, is the colloquial form of Classical miʾzar. ḥawāʾij, “things, gear”, plural of ḥāja.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يَزَالُوا بِهِ حَتَّى أَدْخَلُوهُ الْخَلْوَةَ وَأَطْلَقُوا فِيهَا الْبَخُورَ
sentences.tr: wa-lam yazālū bihi ḥattā adkhalūhu al-khalwata wa-aṭlaqū fīhā al-bakhūra
sentences.l: And they did not cease with him until they made-him-enter the private-room, and set-loose in it the incense.
sentences.i: They kept him moving until they had brought him into the private chamber, and there they lit the incense.
sentences.n: mā zāla bihi, “to keep at someone”, to keep leading him along. khalwa, “privacy”, here the private cubicle of the bath. aṭlaqa al-bakhūr, “to release incense”, to set it smoking.

sentences.t: فَوَجَدَهَا مَلأٰنَةً مِنْ سَائِرِ الْفَوَاكِهِ وَالْمَشْمُومِ وَشَقُّوالَهُ بَطِّيخَةً وَأَجْلَسُوهُ عَلَى كُرْسِيٍّ مِنَ الأَبْنُوسِ
sentences.tr: fa-wajadahā malʾānatan min sāʾiri al-fawākihi wa-al-mashmūmi wa-shaqqū lahu baṭṭīkhatan wa-ajlasūhu ʿalā kursiyyin mina al-abnūsi
sentences.l: And he found it full of all-kinds of the fruits and the things-smelled, and they split for him a melon, and seated-him on a chair of the ebony.
sentences.i: He found it filled with every kind of fruit and fragrant flowers. They cut open a melon for him and seated him on an ebony chair.
sentences.n: malʾāna, “full”, is the post-classical feminine of malʾān (Classical prefers malʾā); the print writes it without the long ā, and the pointing supplies it. mashmūm, “what is smelled”, sweet-scented flowers and herbs. The print runs شقوا and له together as one word; the spacing is kept. The shadda on بطّيخة is the print's; baṭṭīkha is a melon, often the watermelon.

sentences.t: وَوَقَفَ الْبَلَّانُ يَغْسِلُهُ وَالْعَبْدَانِ يَصُبَّانِ الْمَاءَ ثُمَّ دَلَكُوهُ دَلْكًا جَيِّدًا وَقَالُوا لَهُ يَا مَوْلَانَا الصَّاحِبَ نَعِيمٌ دَائِمٌ
sentences.tr: wa-waqafa al-ballānu yaghsiluhu wa-al-ʿabdāni yaṣubbāni al-māʾa thumma dalakūhu dalkan jayyidan wa-qālū lahu yā mawlānā al-ṣāḥiba naʿīmun dāʾimun
sentences.l: And the bath-man stood washing him and the two-slaves pouring the water; then they rubbed-him a good rubbing and said to him: O our lord the Ṣāḥib, bliss lasting!
sentences.i: The attendant stood washing him while the two slaves poured the water; then they gave him a good rubbing down and said to him, “Our lord the Vizier, may your bliss endure!”
sentences.n: dalakūhu dalkan, a cognate accusative, “rubbed him a rubbing”, i.e. thoroughly. al-ṣāḥib, “the companion”, was a title of viziers and high officials, as the next units make plain. naʿīm dāʾim, “lasting bliss!”, is the attendants' wish to a bather on leaving the bath, like Naʿīman! in modern use.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ خَرَجُوا وَرَدُّوا عَلَيْهِ الْبَابَ
sentences.tr: thumma kharajū wa-raddū ʿalayhi al-bāba
sentences.l: Then they went-out and closed upon him the door.
sentences.i: Then they went out and shut the door on him.
sentences.n: radda al-bāba, “to return the door”, i.e. to close it.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا تَخَيَّلَ ذَلِكَ قَامَ وَرَفَعَ الْمِيزَرَ مِنْ وَسَطِهِ وَصَارَ يَضْحَكُ إِلَى أَنْ غُشِيَ عَلَيْهِ وَاسْتَمَرَّ سَاعَةً يَضْحَكُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā takhayyala dhālika qāma wa-rafaʿa al-mīzara min wasaṭihi wa-ṣāra yaḍḥaku ilā an ghushiya ʿalayhi wa-istamarra sāʿatan yaḍḥaku
sentences.l: And when he fancied that, he rose and lifted the waist-wrap from his middle, and took-to laughing until he fainted, and continued an hour laughing.
sentences.i: As he fancied all this, he got up, lifted the wrap from his waist and began to laugh, until he fainted with laughing; and he went on laughing for a long while.
sentences.n: ghushiya ʿalayhi, “he fainted”, passive with ʿalā; here of a fit of laughter. sāʿa, “an hour”, in the Nights usually just “a while”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَٰلَ فِي نَفْسِهِ مَا بَالُهُمْ يُخَاطِبُونَنِي خِطَابَ الْوَزِيرِ وَيَقُولُونَ يَا مَوْلَانَا الصَّاحِبَ
sentences.tr: thumma qāla fī nafsihi mā bāluhum yukhāṭibūnanī khiṭāba al-wazīri wa-yaqūlūna yā mawlānā al-ṣāḥiba
sentences.l: Then he said in himself: What is their case, (that) they address-me (with) the address of the vizier, and say “O our lord the Ṣāḥib”?
sentences.i: Then he said to himself, “What is the matter with them, addressing me as they would the vizier and calling me ‘Our lord the Vizier’?
sentences.n: The print has قل for qāla, a habit of the edition. mā bāluhum, “what is their state?”, i.e. what has got into them. khiṭāba al-wazīri, cognate accusative, “with the address (proper to) the vizier”.

sentences.t: وَلَعَلَّ الأَمْرَ الْتَبَسَ عَلَيْهِمْ فِي هَذِهِ السَّاعَةِ وَبَعْدَ ذَلِكَ يَعْرِفُونَنِي وَيَقُولُونَ هَذَا زَلِيطٌ وَيُشْبِعُونَ صَكًّا فِي رَقَبَتِي
sentences.tr: wa-laʿalla al-amra iltabasa ʿalayhim fī hādhihi al-sāʿati wa-baʿda dhālika yaʿrifūnanī wa-yaqūlūna hādhā Zalīṭun wa-yushbiʿūna ṣakkan fī raqabatī
sentences.l: And perhaps the matter has become-confused for them at this hour, and after that they will know-me and say ‘This is Zalīṭ’, and will give-their-fill of slapping on my neck.”
sentences.i: Perhaps they are confused for the moment; later they will recognize me and say, ‘This is Zalīṭ,’ and slap me round the neck till they are tired of it.”
sentences.n: Zalīṭ is a nickname, not a proper name; it may be from colloquial zalaṭ, “stark naked”, which would make it something like “Bare-bum” or “the penniless one”, but the sense is a guess. iltabasa ʿalā, “to be unclear to, confuse”. ashbaʿa, “to sate, give one's fill”: here “to slap without stinting”. ṣakk, a blow with the flat of the hand; a slap on the back of the neck was the stock humiliation of a buffoon or nobody. The shadda on صكّا is the print's.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُ اسْتَحَمَّى وَفَتَحَ الْبَابَ فَتَخَيَّلَ أَنَّ مَمْلُوكًا صَغِيرًا وَطَوَاشِيًا قَدْ دَخَلَا عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: thumma innahu istaḥammā wa-fataḥa al-bāba fa-takhayyala anna mamlūkan ṣaghīran wa-ṭawāshiyan qad dakhalā ʿalayhi
sentences.l: Then he bathed and opened the door, and fancied that a small mamluk and a eunuch had come-in upon him.
sentences.i: Then he finished bathing and opened the door, and fancied that a young mamluk and a eunuch had come in to him.
sentences.n: istaḥammā, “he bathed”, is the colloquial form of Classical istaḥamma, the doubled verb treated as one with a weak final letter. mamlūk, a slave page; ṭawāshī (from Turkish), a eunuch.

sentences.t: فَالْمَمْلُوكُ مَعَهُ بُقْجَةٌ فَفَتَحَهَا وَأَخْرَجَ مِنْهَا ثَلٰثَ فُوَطٍ مِنَ الْحَرِيرِ فَرَمَى الأُولَى عَلَى رَأْسِهِ وَالأُخْرَى عَلَى أَكْتَافِهِ وَحَزَمَهُ بِالثَّالِثَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-al-mamlūku maʿahu buqjatun fa-fataḥahā wa-akhraja minhā thalātha fuwaṭin mina al-ḥarīri fa-ramā al-ūlā ʿalā raʾsihi wa-al-ukhrā ʿalā aktāfihi wa-ḥazamahu bi-al-thālithati
sentences.l: And the mamluk, with him a bundle; and he opened it and brought-out from it three towels of the silk, and threw the first on his head and the other on his shoulders, and girded-him with the third.
sentences.i: The mamluk had a bundle with him; he opened it and took out three silk towels. He threw the first over the man's head and the second over his shoulders, and girded him with the third.
sentences.n: buqja (from Turkish bohça), a cloth bundle for clothes. fūṭa, plural fuwaṭ, a towel or wrap of the bath. thalātha is printed ثلٰث, with a dagger alif for the long ā, the edition's spelling. al-ukhrā, “the other”, stands here for “the second”, as in colloquial usage. aktāf, “shoulders”, plural for dual, as often.

sentences.t: وَقَدَّمَ لَهُ الطَّوَاشِي قَبْقَابًا فَلَبِسَهُ وَأَقْبَلَتْ عَلَيْهِ مَمَالِيكُ وَطَوَاشِيَةٌ وَصَارُوا يُسْنِدُونَهُ
sentences.tr: wa-qaddama lahu al-ṭawāshī qabqāban fa-labisahu wa-aqbalat ʿalayhi mamālīku wa-ṭawāshiyatun wa-ṣārū yusnidūnahu
sentences.l: And the eunuch presented to him wooden-clogs, and he put-them-on; and there came-towards him mamluks and eunuchs, and they took-to propping-him-up.
sentences.i: The eunuch set a pair of bath clogs before him and he put them on. Then mamluks and eunuchs came up to him and began to support him on either side.
sentences.n: qabqāb, the high wooden clog worn in the bath to keep the feet off the wet floor. ṭawāshiya, a colloquial plural of ṭawāshī. asnada, “to prop up, support”: great men were held up by the arms by their servants as they left the bath.

sentences.t: وَكُلُّ ذَلِكَ حَصَلَ وَهُوَ يَضْحَكُ إِلَى أَنْ خَرَجَ وَطَلَعَ اللِّيوَانَ
sentences.tr: wa-kullu dhālika ḥaṣala wa-huwa yaḍḥaku ilā an kharaja wa-ṭalaʿa al-līwāna
sentences.l: And all that happened while he was laughing, until he went-out and went-up (to) the hall.
sentences.i: And through all of this he never stopped laughing, until he had come out and gone up into the hall.
sentences.n: līwān, the colloquial form of īwān, a raised hall or dais open on one side; in a bath it is the raised outer hall where bathers rest. ṭalaʿa, “to go up”, here takes the place gone up to as a direct object, without ilā.

sentences.t: فَوَجَدَ فَرْشًا عَظِيمًا لَا يَصْلُحُ إِلَّا لِلْمُلُوكِ وَتَبَادَرَتْ إِلَيْهِ الْغِلْمَانُ وَأَجْلَسُوهُ عَلَي الْمَرْتَبَةِ وَصَارُوا يَكْبِسُونَهُ حَتَّى غَلَبَ عَلَيْهِ النَّوْمُ
sentences.tr: fa-wajada farshan ʿaẓīman lā yaṣluḥu illā li-al-mulūki wa-tabādarat ilayhi al-ghilmānu wa-ajlasūhu ʿalā al-martabati wa-ṣārū yakbisūnahu ḥattā ghalaba ʿalayhi al-nawmu
sentences.l: And he found furnishings magnificent, not fitting except for the kings; and the pages hastened to him and seated-him on the mattress, and took-to kneading-him until sleep overcame him.
sentences.i: There he found furnishings so splendid that they were fit only for kings. The pages hurried to him, seated him on the couch, and began to massage him until sleep overcame him.
sentences.n: farsh, “furnishings”, carpets and cushions spread on the floor. li-, “for”: lā yaṣluḥu illā li-al-mulūk, “is fit only for kings”. tabādarat ilayhi al-ghilmānu: a broken plural of persons takes a feminine verb. martaba, a mattress or raised seat of honour. The print writes ʿalā as علي here.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا نَامَ رَأَى فِي حِضْنِهِ صَبِيَّةً فَبَاسَهَا وَوَضَعَهَا بَيْنَ فَخِذَيْهِ وَجَلَسَ مِنْهَا مَجْلِسَ الرَّجُلِ مِنَ الْمَرْأَةِ وَقَبَضَ ذَكَرَهُ بِيَدِهِ وَسَحَبَهَا عِنْدَهُ وَعَصَرَهَا تَحْتَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā nāma raʾā fī ḥiḍnihi ṣabiyyatan fa-bāsahā wa-waḍaʿahā bayna fakhidhayhi wa-jalasa minhā majlisa al-rajuli mina al-marʾati wa-qabaḍa dhakarahu bi-yadihi wa-saḥabahā ʿindahu wa-ʿaṣarahā taḥtahu
sentences.l: And when he slept, he saw in his embrace a girl, and he kissed her and put her between his thighs, and sat from her the sitting of the man from the woman, and grasped his penis in his hand and drew her to him and pressed her beneath him.
sentences.i: And when he fell asleep he dreamed there was a girl in his arms. He kissed her and set her between his thighs, and sat to her as a man sits to a woman; he took his penis in his hand, drew her to him, and pressed her down beneath him.
sentences.n: raʾā, “saw”, here “saw in a dream”. bāsa, “to kiss”, colloquial for Classical qabbala. jalasa minhā majlisa al-rajuli mina al-marʾati, “sat to her the sitting of a man to a woman”, a stock phrase for taking position to have intercourse; majlisa is a cognate accusative. dhakar, “the male member”.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا بِوَاحِدٍ يَقُولُ لَهُ انْتَبِهْ يَا زَلِيطُ قَدْ جَاءَ الظُّهْرُ وَأَنْتَ نَائِمٌ
sentences.tr: wa-idhā bi-wāḥidin yaqūlu lahu intabih yā Zalīṭu qad jāʾa al-ẓuhru wa-anta nāʾimun
sentences.l: And behold, someone saying to him: Wake-up, O Zalīṭ! The noon has come, and you are asleep.
sentences.i: And suddenly someone was saying to him, “Wake up, Zalīṭ! It's noon already, and you still asleep!”
sentences.n: wa-idhā bi-, “and behold”: the bi- only marks who appears. wa-anta nāʾimun, “while you are asleep”, a circumstantial clause with wa-.

sentences.t: فَفَتَحَ عَيْنَهُ فَوَجَدَ رُوحَهُ عَلَى الْحَوْضِ الْبَارِدِ وَحَوْلَهُ جَمَاعَةٌ يَضْحَكُونَ عَلَيْهِ وَأَيْرُهُ قَائِمٌ وَالْفُوطَةُ انْحَلَّتْ مِنْ وَسَطِهِ وَتَبَيَّنَ لَهُ أَنَّ كُلَّ هَذِهِ أَضْغَاثُ أَحْلَامٍ وَتَخَيُّلَاتُ حَشِيشٍ
sentences.tr: fa-fataḥa ʿaynahu fa-wajada rūḥahu ʿalā al-ḥawḍi al-bāridi wa-ḥawlahu jamāʿatun yaḍḥakūna ʿalayhi wa-ayruhu qāʾimun wa-al-fūṭatu inḥallat min wasaṭihi wa-tabayyana lahu anna kulla hādhihi aḍghāthu aḥlāmin wa-takhayyulātu ḥashīshin
sentences.l: And he opened his eye and found his soul (= himself) at the cold basin, and around him a company laughing at him, and his prick standing, and the towel had come-undone from his middle; and it became-clear to him that all of this was jumbles of dreams and fancies of hashish.
sentences.i: He opened his eyes and found himself lying by the cold-water basin, with a crowd of people round him laughing at him: his prick was standing up and the towel had slipped from his waist. Then it dawned on him that all of it had been a muddle of dreams and the fancies of hashish.
sentences.n: rūḥahu, “his soul”, is the colloquial reflexive, “himself” (Classical nafsahu). ḍaḥika ʿalā, “to laugh at”. ayr is the blunt everyday word for the penis, and the text uses it without embarrassment. fūṭa, the cloth wrapped round the waist in the bath. aḍghāthu aḥlāmin, “confused bundles of dreams”, is a Qurʾānic phrase (Sūrat Yūsuf 12:44).

sentences.t: فَاغْتَمَّ وَنَظَرَ إِلَى الَّذِي نَبَّهَهُ وَقَالَ كُنْتَ اصْبِرْ حَتَّى أَحُطَّهُ
sentences.tr: fa-ightamma wa-naẓara ilā alladhī nabbahahu wa-qāla kunta iṣbir ḥattā aḥuṭṭahu
sentences.l: And he grew-sad and looked at the-one who had woken him and said: You-should-have waited until I put it (in)!
sentences.i: He was vexed, and he looked at the man who had woken him and said, “You might have waited till I had put it in!”
sentences.n: kunta iṣbir, “you should have been waiting”, is read here as the colloquial pattern of kunt with an imperative, a reproach for what was not done; the print could also be read kuntu aṣbiru, “I would have waited”, which makes poorer sense. ḥaṭṭa, “to put, set down”, is everyday Middle Arabic for Classical waḍaʿa. The print marks the doubled bāʾ of nabbahahu, “he woke him”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ النَّاسُ أَمَا تَسْتَحِي يَا حَشَّاشُ وَأَنْتَ نَائِمٌ وَذَكَرُكَ قَائِمٌ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-nāsu amā tastaḥī yā ḥashshāshu wa-anta nāʾimun wa-dhakaruka qāʾimun
sentences.l: And the people said to him: Are-you not ashamed, O hashish-eater, while you are asleep and your member is standing?
sentences.i: The people said to him, “Have you no shame, you hashish-eater, lying asleep with your member standing up?”
sentences.n: ḥashshāsh, “hashish-eater”, a word of contempt; nāʾimun / qāʾimun make a jingle. tastaḥī is the usual spelling of tastaḥyī, “you feel shame”.

sentences.t: وَصَكُّوهُ حَتَّى احْمَرَّ قَفَاهُ وَهُوَ جِيعَانُ وَقَدْ ذَاقَ طَعْمَ السَّعَادَةِ وَهُوَ فِى الْمَنَامِ
sentences.tr: wa-ṣakkūhu ḥattā iḥmarra qafāhu wa-huwa jīʿānu wa-qad dhāqa ṭaʿma al-saʿādati wa-huwa fī al-manāmi
sentences.l: And they slapped him until his nape went-red, and he hungry, and he had tasted the taste of happiness while he was in sleep.
sentences.i: And they slapped him on the back of the neck till it was red, hungry as he was, though he had tasted bliss in his dream.
sentences.n: ṣakka, “to strike, slap”; a slap on the qafā, the back of the neck, is the classic humiliation of the buffoon. jīʿān, “hungry”, is Middle Arabic for Classical jāʾiʿ; it is pointed here as a diptote (jīʿānu), like other adjectives of the faʿlān pattern.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ مِنَ الْجَارِيَةِ هَذَا الْكَلَامَ ضَحِكَ حَتَّى اسْتَلْقَى عَلَى قَفَاهُ وَقَالَ لِبَاكُونَ يَا دَادَتِي إِنَّ هَذَا حَدِيثٌ عَجِيبٌ فَإِنِّي مَا سَمِعْتُ مِثْلَ هَذِهِ الْحِكَايَةِ فَهَلْ عِنْدَكِ غَيْرُهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa Kāna Mā Kāna mina al-jāriyati hādhā al-kalāma ḍaḥika ḥattā istalqā ʿalā qafāhu wa-qāla li-Bākūna yā dādatī inna hādhā ḥadīthun ʿajībun fa-innī mā samiʿtu mithla hādhihi al-ḥikāyati fa-hal ʿindaki ghayruhā
sentences.l: And when Kān Mā Kān heard from the slave-woman these words, he laughed until he lay-back on his nape, and said to Bākūn: O my nurse, this is a wondrous tale, for I have not heard the like of this story; so is there with you another-than-it?
sentences.i: When Kān Mā Kān heard this from the slave-woman, he laughed till he fell over on his back, and said to Bākūn, “Nanny, that is a marvellous tale! I have never heard a story like it. Do you know another?”
sentences.n: istalqā ʿalā qafāhu, “he lay back on the nape of his neck”, the stock phrase for helpless laughter. dāda, “nurse, nanny”, a Persian loanword (dāya) used in Egypt for the woman who brings up a child. fa-hal ʿindaki ghayruhā, literally “is there with you other than it?”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ نَعَمْ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu naʿam
sentences.l: And she said to him: Yes.
sentences.i: “Yes,” she said.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْجَارِيَةَ بَاكُونَ لَمْ تَزَلْ تُحَدِّثُ كَانَ مَا كَانَ بِمَخَارِفِ حِكَايَاتٍ وَنَوَادِرَ مُضْحِكَاتٍ حَتَّى غَلَبَ عَلَيْهِ النَّوْمُ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-jāriyata Bākūna lam tazal tuḥaddithu Kāna Mā Kāna bi-makhārifi ḥikāyātin wa-nawādira muḍḥikātin ḥattā ghalaba ʿalayhi al-nawmu
sentences.l: Then the slave-woman Bākūn did not cease telling Kān Mā Kān fanciful-ones of stories and laughable rare-tales, until sleep overcame him.
sentences.i: And the slave-woman Bākūn went on telling Kān Mā Kān fanciful stories and comic anecdotes until sleep overcame him.
sentences.n: makhārif is doubtful. It is read here as a plural akin to khurāfa, “fable, idle tale”, so “fables of stories”; it may instead be a misprint for zakhārif, “ornaments, embellished tales”. ḥaddatha bi-, “to tell someone (of) something”: the bi- carries what is told. nawādir, “rare things”, hence “witty anecdotes”; ḥikāyātin / muḍḥikātin rhyme.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ تَزَلْ تِلْكَ الْجَارِيَةُ جَالِسَةً عِنْدَ رَاسِهِ حَتَّى مَضَى غَالِبُ اللَّيْلِ
sentences.tr: wa-lam tazal tilka al-jāriyatu jālisatan ʿinda rāsihi ḥattā maḍā ghālibu al-layli
sentences.l: And that slave-woman did not cease sitting at his head until the greater-part of the night had passed.
sentences.i: The slave-woman stayed sitting by his head until most of the night had gone by.
sentences.n: rās, “head”, is spelt and pointed as the print gives it, without hamza (Classical raʾs). ghālib al-layl, “the most of the night”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ فِي نَفْسِهَا هَذَا وَقْتُ انْتِهَازِ الْفُرْصَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat fī nafsihā hādhā waqtu intihāzi al-furṣati
sentences.l: And she said in herself: This is the time of seizing the opportunity.
sentences.i: Then she said to herself, “Now is the time to seize my chance.”
sentences.n: intahaza al-furṣa, “to seize the opportunity”, a fixed phrase.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ نَهَضَتْ وَسَلَّتِ الْخَنْجَرَ وَوَثَبَتْ عَلَى كَانَ مَا كَانَ وَأَرَادَتْ ذَبْحَهُ
sentences.tr: thumma nahaḍat wa-sallati al-khanjara wa-wathabat ʿalā Kāna Mā Kāna wa-arādat dhabḥahu
sentences.l: Then she rose and drew the dagger and leapt upon Kān Mā Kān and wished his slaughtering.
sentences.i: She got up, drew the dagger, sprang at Kān Mā Kān and was about to cut his throat,
sentences.n: The print has ووثبث, a misprint for ووثبت, corrected here. The print marks the doubled lām of sallat, “she drew (the blade)”. dhabaḥa, “to slaughter”, properly to cut the throat as one does a sheep.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا بِأُمِّ كَانَ مَا كَانَ دَخَلَتْ عَلَيْهِمَا
sentences.tr: wa-idhā bi-ummi Kāna Mā Kāna dakhalat ʿalayhimā
sentences.l: And behold, the mother of Kān Mā Kān came-in upon the two of them.
sentences.i: when all at once Kān Mā Kān's mother came in on the two of them.
sentences.n: wa-idhā bi-, “and behold”: the bi- only marks who appears. Kān Mā Kān's mother is the widow of Ḍawʾ al-Makān.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَتْهَا بَاكُونُ قَامَتْ لَهَا وَاسْتَقْبَلَتْهَا ثُمَّ لَحِقَهَا الْخَوْفُ فَصَارَتْ تَنْتَفِضُ كَأَنَّهَا أَخَذَتْهَا الْحُمَّى
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾathā Bākūnu qāmat lahā wa-istaqbalathā thumma laḥiqahā al-khawfu fa-ṣārat tantafiḍu ka-annahā akhadhathā al-ḥummā
sentences.l: And when Bākūn saw her she stood for her and received her; then fear overtook her, and she began trembling as-though the fever had taken her.
sentences.i: When Bākūn saw her she rose to greet her and went to meet her; but then fear came over her, and she began to shake as if gripped by a fever.
sentences.n: qāma la-, “to stand up for someone”, the courtesy shown on a superior's entrance. intafaḍa, “to shake, tremble”, used of a fever fit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَتْهَا أُمُّ كَانَ مَا كَانَ تَعَجَّبَتْ وَنَبَّهَتْ وَلَدَهَا مِنَ النَّوْمِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾathā ummu Kāna Mā Kāna taʿajjabat wa-nabbahat waladahā mina al-nawmi
sentences.l: And when the mother of Kān Mā Kān saw her she wondered, and woke her son from sleep.
sentences.i: Kān Mā Kān's mother was astonished at the sight of her, and roused her son from his sleep.
sentences.n: The print marks the doubled bāʾ of nabbahat, “she woke”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا اسْتَيْقَظَ وَجَدَهَا جَالِسَةً فَوْقَ رَاسِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā istayqaẓa wajadahā jālisatan fawqa rāsihi
sentences.l: And when he awoke he found her sitting above his head.
sentences.i: When he awoke he found her sitting at his head.
sentences.n: The print has وجداه, a misprint for وجدها, corrected here. “Her” is his mother, sitting at his pillow; fawqa rāsihi, literally “above his head”, means at the head of the bed.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ السَّبَبُ فِي حَيَاتِهِ مَجِيئَهَا
sentences.tr: wa-kāna al-sababu fī ḥayātihi majīʾahā
sentences.l: And the cause in his life (= of his staying alive) was her coming.
sentences.i: It was her coming that saved his life.
sentences.n: Word order: the subject of kāna is al-sabab, and majīʾahā, “her coming”, is its predicate in the accusative, put last for weight; one might equally read it the other way round. fī here gives the reason, “the cause for his life”.

sentences.t: وَسَبَبُ مَجِيءِ أُمِّهِ إِلَيْهِ أَنَّ قَضَى فَكَانَ سَمِعَتِ الْحَدِيثَ وَالِاتِّفَاقَ عَلَى قَتْلِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-sababu majīʾi ummihi ilayhi anna Qaḍā Fakāna samiʿati al-ḥadītha wa-al-ittifāqa ʿalā qatlihi
sentences.l: And the cause of his mother's coming to him was that Qaḍā Fakān had heard the talk and the agreement on his killing.
sentences.i: The reason his mother had come to him was that Qaḍā Fakān had overheard the conversation and the plot to kill him.
sentences.n: The print sets the name as two words, قضى فكان, Qaḍā Fakān (“Fate has decreed, and it came to be”); she is Sharrukān's daughter, Kān Mā Kān's cousin. anna is followed by a name that cannot show its case; ittifāq ʿalā, “agreement on”, here “the plot to”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لِأُمِّهِ يَا زَوْجَةَ عَمِّى الْحَقِي وَلَدَكِ قَبْلَ أَنْ تَقْتُلَهُ الْعَاهِرَةُ بَاكُونُ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat li-ummihi yā zawjata ʿammī ilḥaqī waladaki qabla an taqtulahu al-ʿāhiratu Bākūnu
sentences.l: And she said to his mother: O wife of my uncle, catch-up-with your son before the whore Bākūn kills him!
sentences.i: She said to his mother, “Aunt, go quickly to your son before that whore Bākūn kills him!”
sentences.n: The print has ياكرن, a misprint for باكون, corrected here. zawjat ʿammī, “my paternal uncle's wife”: Kān Mā Kān's father Ḍawʾ al-Makān was the brother of her father Sharrukān. ilḥaqī, “overtake, reach in time”. ʿāhira, “harlot”, a plain insult.

sentences.t: وَأَخْبَرَتْهَا بِمَا جَرَى مِنْ أَوَّلِهِ إِلَى آخِرِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-akhbarathā bi-mā jarā min awwalihi ilā ākhirihi
sentences.l: And she informed her of what had happened, from its first to its last.
sentences.i: And she told her everything that had happened from beginning to end.
sentences.n: akhbara bi-, “to inform of”: the verb takes the news with bi-.

sentences.t: فَخَرَجَتْ وَهِيَ لَا تَعْقِلُ وَلَاتَنْتَظِرُ شَيْأً حَتَّى دَخَلَتْ فِى السَّاعَةِ الَّتِي نَامَ فِيهَا وَهَمَّتْ بَاكُونُ عَلَيْهِ تُرِيدُ ذَبْحَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-kharajat wa-hiya lā taʿqilu wa-lā tantaẓiru shayʾan ḥattā dakhalat fī al-sāʿati allatī nāma fīhā wa-hammat Bākūnu ʿalayhi turīdu dhabḥahu
sentences.l: And she went-out, not in-her-wits and not waiting for a thing, until she entered in the hour in which he slept and Bākūn made-to-fall upon him, wishing his slaughtering.
sentences.i: Out she went, beside herself, waiting for nothing, and she came in at the very hour when he had fallen asleep and Bākūn was bending over him to cut his throat.
sentences.n: lā taʿqilu, “she did not reason”, i.e. was out of her mind with fear. The print runs ولا تنتظر together as one word, ولاتنتظر. shayʾan is written with hamza on an alif seat, شيأ, as before. hamma bi- is Classical for “to be on the point of”; hamma ʿalā here is looser, “to fall on, go for”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا اسْتَيْقَظَهُ قَالَ لِأُمِّهِ لَقَدْ جِئْتِ يَا أُمِّي فِي وَقْتٍ طَيِّبٍ وَدَادَتِي بَاكُونُ حَاضِرَةٌ عِنْدِى فِي تِلْكَ اللَّيْلَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā istayqaẓahu qāla li-ummihi la-qad jiʾti yā ummī fī waqtin ṭayyibin wa-dādatī Bākūnu ḥāḍiratun ʿindī fī tilka al-laylati
sentences.l: And when it woke him (?), he said to his mother: You have come, O my mother, at a good time, and my nurse Bākūn present with me on that night.
sentences.i: When he was woken, he said to his mother, “You have come at a good time, Mother, with my nanny Bākūn here with me tonight.”
sentences.n: istayqaẓahu is odd: istayqaẓa, “to wake up”, does not take an object. Most likely the print means either istayqaẓa, “he woke”, with a stray hāʾ, or ayqaẓathu, “she woke him”; it is kept as printed, and taken in the sense “when he was awake”. fī tilka al-layla, “on that night”, where we would say “tonight”. He notices nothing.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُ الْتَفَتَ إِلَى بَاكُونَ وَقَالَ لَهَا بِحَيَاتِي عَلَيْكِ هَلْ تَعْرِفِينَ حِكَايَةً أَحْسَنَ مِنَ الْحِكَايَاتِ الَّتِي حَدَّثْتِنِي بِهَا
sentences.tr: thumma innahu iltafata ilā Bākūna wa-qāla lahā bi-ḥayātī ʿalayki hal taʿrifīna ḥikāyatan aḥsana mina al-ḥikāyāti allatī ḥaddathtinī bihā
sentences.l: Then he turned to Bākūn and said to her: By my life upon you, do you know a story finer than the stories which you told me?
sentences.i: Then he turned to Bākūn and said, “On my life, I beg you: do you know a better story than the ones you have been telling me?”
sentences.n: bi-ḥayātī ʿalayki, “by my life (I lay it) upon you”, a coaxing form of entreaty.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ الْجَارِيَةُ وَأَيْنَ مَاحَدَّثْتُكَ بِهِ سَابِقًا مِمَّا أُحَدِّثُكَ بِهِ الْآنَ فَإِنَّهُ أَعْذَبُ وَلَكِنْ أَحْكِيهِ لَكَ فِي غَيْرِ هَذَا الْوَقْتِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu al-jāriyatu wa-ayna mā ḥaddathtuka bihi sābiqan mimmā uḥaddithuka bihi al-āna fa-innahu aʿdhabu wa-lākin aḥkīhi laka fī ghayri hādhā al-waqti
sentences.l: And the slave-woman said to him: And where is what I told you before from what I will tell you now? For it is sweeter; but I will tell it to you at another-than this time.
sentences.i: The slave-woman answered, “What I have told you so far is nothing to what I could tell you now: that one is sweeter still. But I will tell it you some other time.”
sentences.n: wa-ayna X min Y, “where is X from Y?”, i.e. X is nothing beside Y. The print runs ما حدثتك together as ماحدثتك. aḥkīhi, “I shall tell it”: the imperfect serves for the future.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَامَتْ بَاكُونُ وَهِيَ لَا تُصَدِّقُ بِالنَّجَاةِ
sentences.tr: thumma qāmat Bākūnu wa-hiya lā tuṣaddiqu bi-al-najāti
sentences.l: Then Bākūn rose, and she not believing in the escape.
sentences.i: Then Bākūn got up, scarcely able to believe she had escaped.
sentences.n: lā tuṣaddiqu bi-, “not believing in”, here “hardly believing her luck”: ṣaddaqa takes what is believed with bi-.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا مَعَ السَّلَامَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā maʿa al-salāmati
sentences.l: And he said to her: With safety.
sentences.i: “Go safely,” he said to her.
sentences.n: maʿa al-salāma, “(go) with safety”, the everyday farewell, still used today.

sentences.t: وَلَمَحَتْ بِمَكْرِهَا أَنَّ أُمَّهُ عِنْدَهَا خَبَرٌ بِمَا حَصَلَ فَذَهَبَتْ إِلَى حَالِهَا
sentences.tr: wa-lamaḥat bi-makrihā anna ummahu ʿindahā khabarun bi-mā ḥaṣala fa-dhahabat ilā ḥālihā
sentences.l: And she glimpsed by her cunning that his mother had with her news of what had happened; and she went to her state (= her own way).
sentences.i: With her cunning she had seen that his mother knew what had happened, and she went off about her business.
sentences.n: lamaḥa, “to catch a glimpse of”, here “to sense”. ʿindahā khabarun bi-, literally “with her is news of”, “she knew about”. dhahaba ilā ḥālihi, “to go to one's own affairs”, i.e. to go away.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذَلِكَ قَالَتْ لَهُ وَالِدَتُهُ يَا وَلَدِي هَذِهِ لَيْلَةٌ مُبَارَكَةٌ حَيْثُ نَجَّاكَ اللّٰهُ تَعَالَى مِنْ هَذِهِ الْمَلْعُونَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika qālat lahu wālidatuhu yā waladī hādhihi laylatun mubārakatun ḥaythu najjāka Allāhu taʿālā min hādhihi al-malʿūnati
sentences.l: And at that his mother said to him: O my son, this is a blessed night, since God (exalted is He) has saved you from this accursed-one.
sentences.i: Then his mother said to him, “My son, this is a blessed night, for God Most High has delivered you from that accursed woman.”
sentences.n: ḥaythu, properly “where”, is used here for “since, because”, a common late usage. najjā, “to rescue, deliver”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا وَكَيْفَ ذَلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā wa-kayfa dhālika
sentences.l: And he said to her: And how is that?
sentences.i: “How so?” he asked her.

sentences.t: فَأَخْبَرَتْهُ بِالْأَمْرِ مِنْ أَوَّلِهِ إِلَى آخِرِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-akhbarathu bi-al-amri min awwalihi ilā ākhirihi
sentences.l: And she informed him of the matter from its first to its last.
sentences.i: And she told him the whole affair from beginning to end.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا يَا وَالِدَتِي إِنَّ الْحَيَّ مَا لَهُ قَاتِلٌ وَإِنْ قُتِلَ لَايَمُوتُ وَلَكِنِ الْأَحْوَطُ لَنَا أَنَّنَا نَرْحَلُ مِنْ عِنْدِ هَؤُلَاءِ الْأَعْدَاءِ وَاللّٰهُ يَفْعَلُ مَا يُرِيدُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā yā wālidatī inna al-ḥayya mā lahu qātilun wa-in qutila lā yamūtu wa-lākini al-aḥwaṭu lanā annanā narḥalu min ʿindi hāʾulāʾi al-aʿdāʾi wa-Allāhu yafʿalu mā yurīdu
sentences.l: And he said to her: O my mother, the living-one has no killer, and if he is killed he does not die; but the most-cautious for us is that we depart from among these enemies, and God does what He wills.
sentences.i: He said to her, “Mother, a man whose time has not come has no one who can kill him, and even if he is struck down he will not die. Still, the safest course for us is to leave these enemies of ours. God does as He wills.”
sentences.n: The saying means that no one dies before his appointed hour. The print runs لا يموت together as لايموت. al-aḥwaṭ, “the most prudent”. annanā narḥalu, “that we depart”, uses anna with a full clause where Classical would say an narḥala; this is Middle Arabic.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَصْبَحَ الصَّبَاحُ خَرَجَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ مِنَ الْمَدِينَةِ وَاجْتَمَعَ بِالْوَزِيرِ دَنْدَانَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā aṣbaḥa al-ṣabāḥu kharaja Kāna Mā Kāna mina al-madīnati wa-ijtamaʿa bi-al-wazīri Dandāna
sentences.l: And when the morning morninged, Kān Mā Kān went-out from the city and met with the vizier Dandān.
sentences.i: In the morning Kān Mā Kān left the city and joined the vizier Dandān.
sentences.n: aṣbaḥa al-ṣabāḥu, “the morning dawned”, a stock jingle. ijtamaʿa bi-, “to meet with, join”.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ خُرُوجِهِ حَصَلَتْ أُمُورٌ بَيْنَ الْمَلِكِ سَاسَانَ وَنُزْهَةِ الزَّمَانِ أَوْجَبَتْ خُرُوجَ نُزْهَةِ الزَّمَانِ أَيْضًا مِنَ الْمَدِينَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda khurūjihi ḥaṣalat umūrun bayna al-maliki Sāsāna wa-Nuzhati al-Zamāni awjabat khurūja Nuzhati al-Zamāni ayḍan mina al-madīnati
sentences.l: And after his going-out, matters came-about between King Sāsān and Nuzhat al-Zamān that necessitated the going-out of Nuzhat al-Zamān too from the city.
sentences.i: After he had gone, things passed between King Sāsān and Nuzhat al-Zamān that obliged Nuzhat al-Zamān to leave the city as well.
sentences.n: ḥaṣala, “to happen, come about”, is the workhorse verb of Middle Arabic narrative. Nuzhat al-Zamān is Sāsān's wife.

sentences.t: فَاجْتَمَعَتْ بِهِمْ وَاجْتَمَعَ عَلَيْهِمْ جَمِيعُ أَرْبَابِ دَوْلَةِ الْمَلِكِ سَاسَانَ الَّذِينَ يَمِيلُونَ إِلَيْهِمْ
sentences.tr: fa-ijtamaʿat bihim wa-ijtamaʿa ʿalayhim jamīʿu arbābi dawlati al-maliki Sāsāna alladhīna yamīlūna ilayhim
sentences.l: And she joined with them, and there gathered to them all the lords of the state of King Sāsān who inclined towards them.
sentences.i: She joined them, and all the officers of King Sāsān's state who favoured their side gathered round them.
sentences.n: arbāb al-dawla, “the masters of the state”, the great officers of the realm. ijtamaʿa ʿalā, “to rally round”.

sentences.t: فَجَلَسُوا يُدَبِّرُونَ الْحِيلَةَ فَأَجْمَعَ رَأْيُهُمْ عَلَى غَزْوِ مَلِكِ الرُّومِ وَأَخْذِ الثَّأْرِ
sentences.tr: fa-jalasū yudabbirūna al-ḥīlata fa-ajmaʿa raʾyuhum ʿalā ghazwi maliki al-Rūmi wa-akhdhi al-thaʾri
sentences.l: And they sat devising the stratagem, and their opinion was-unanimous on raiding the king of the Rūm and taking the blood-revenge.
sentences.i: They sat down to plan what to do, and they were all agreed on marching against the king of the Rūm and taking revenge.
sentences.n: dabbara al-ḥīla, “to work out a plan”. ajmaʿa raʾyuhum ʿalā, “their opinion was united upon”: Classical says ajmaʿū ʿalā, with the people as subject. al-thaʾr, “blood-revenge”: the print writes it without the hamza, الثار. The revenge is for King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān and Sharrukān.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ تَوَجَّهُوا إِلَى غَزْوِ الرُّومِ وَوَقَعُوا فِي أَسْرِ الْمَلِكِ رُومْزَانَ مَلِكِ الرُّومِ بَعْدَ أُمُورٍ يَطُولُ شَرْحُهَا كَمَا يَظْهَرُ مِنَ السِّيَاقِ
sentences.tr: thumma tawajjahū ilā ghazwi al-Rūmi wa-waqaʿū fī asri al-maliki Rūmzāna maliki al-Rūmi baʿda umūrin yaṭūlu sharḥuhā kamā yaẓharu mina al-siyāqi
sentences.l: Then they set-out to raid the Rūm, and fell into the captivity of King Rūmzān, king of the Rūm, after matters whose explaining is long, as appears from the sequence (of the story).
sentences.i: Then they set out to make war on the Rūm, and after events too long to tell they fell captive to King Rūmzān, king of the Rūm, as the course of the story will show.
sentences.n: Rūmzān is a new name here. The narrator races ahead and gives the outcome first; kamā yaẓharu mina al-siyāq, “as appears from the sequence”, promises that the story will tell it in full. yaṭūlu sharḥuhā, “whose telling grows long”, is a stock formula for skipping events.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَصْبَحَ الصَّبَاحُ أَمَرَ الْمَلِكُ رُومْزَانُ أَنْ يُحْضَرَ كَانَ مَاكَانَ وَالْوَزِيرُ دَنْدَانُ وَجَمَاعَتُهُمَا فَحَضَرُوا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ وَأَجْلَسَهُمْ بِجَانِبِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā aṣbaḥa al-ṣabāḥu amara al-maliku Rūmzānu an yuḥḍara Kāna Mā Kāna wa-al-wazīru Dandānu wa-jamāʿatuhumā fa-ḥaḍarū bayna yadayhi wa-ajlasahum bi-jānibihi
sentences.l: And when the morning dawned, King Rūmzān commanded that Kān Mā Kān be brought, and the vizier Dandān and their company; and they came before him, and he seated them at his side.
sentences.i: When morning came, King Rūmzān gave orders for Kān Mā Kān, the vizier Dandān and their company to be brought to him. They were led into his presence, and he seated them beside him.
sentences.n: The print sets the hero's name as kāna mākāna, run together as it often is. an yuḥḍara, “that (he) be brought”, read as passive; jamāʿatuhumā, “the company of the two of them”, the dual pronoun pointing back to Kān Mā Kān and Dandān. bayna yadayhi, “between his two hands”: into his presence.

sentences.t: وَأَمَرَ بِإِحْضَارِ الْمَوَائِدِ فَأُحْضِرَتْ فَأَكَلُوا وَشَرِبُوا وَاطْمَأَنُّوا بَعْدَ أَنْ أَيْقَنُوا بِالْمَوْتِ لَمَّا أَمَرَ بِإِحْضَارِهِمْ
sentences.tr: wa-amara bi-iḥḍāri al-mawāʾidi fa-uḥḍirat fa-akalū wa-sharibū wa-iṭmaʾannū baʿda an ayqanū bi-al-mawti lammā amara bi-iḥḍārihim
sentences.l: And he commanded the bringing of the tables, and they were brought, and they ate and drank and were-reassured, after they had been-certain of death when he commanded their being-brought.
sentences.i: Then he ordered the tables to be set, and they were brought, and the captives ate and drank and took heart, though when he had sent for them they had been sure they were going to their deaths.
sentences.n: amara bi-, “to give orders for”: the verb takes its object with bi-. māʾida, plural mawāʾid, a table spread with food. iṭmaʾanna, “to be at rest, feel safe”. ayqana bi-, “to be certain of”, again with bi- chosen by the verb.

sentences.t: وَقَالُوا لِبَعْضِهِمْ إِنَّهُ مَا أَرْسَلَ إِلَيْنَا إِلَّا لِأَنَّهُ يُرِيدُ قَتْلَنَا
sentences.tr: wa-qālū li-baʿḍihim innahu mā arsala ilaynā illā li-annahu yurīdu qatlanā
sentences.l: And they said to some-of-them: Truly he has not sent for us except because he wants our killing.
sentences.i: They had said to one another, “He has sent for us only because he means to kill us.”
sentences.n: qālū li-baʿḍihim, “they said to some of them”: the spoken way of saying “to one another”, where Classical prose has qāla baʿḍuhum li-baʿḍin. arsala ilā, “to send to”, here “to send for”. mā … illā, “not … except”: “only”.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ أَنِ اطْمَأَنُّوا قَالَ لَهُمُ الْمَلِكُ إِنِّي رَأَيْتُ مَنَامًا وَقَصَصْتُهُ عَلَى الرُّهْبَانِ فَقَالُوا مَا يُفَسِّرُهُ لَكَ إِلَّا الْوَزِيرُ دَنْدَانُ
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda an iṭmaʾannū qāla lahumu al-maliku innī raʾaytu manāman wa-qaṣaṣtuhu ʿalā al-ruhbāni fa-qālū mā yufassiruhu laka illā al-wazīru Dandānu
sentences.l: And after they were-reassured, the king said to them: I have seen a dream, and I related it to the monks, and they said: None interprets it for you but the vizier Dandān.
sentences.i: When they were at ease, the king said to them, “I have had a dream. I told it to the monks, and they said that no one could interpret it for me but the vizier Dandān.”
sentences.n: The print has رابت, a misprint for رايت (raʾaytu, “I saw”), corrected here. Here the print spells iṭmaʾannū without its hamza (اطمانوا), two lines after printing it in full. manām, “sleep”, and so “a dream”. qaṣṣa ʿalā, “to relate to”. fassara, “to explain, interpret”, the regular verb for reading dreams.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْوَزِيرُ خَيْرًا رَأَيْتَ يَا مَلِكَ الزَّمَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-wazīru khayran raʾayta yā malika al-zamāni
sentences.l: And the vizier said to him: Good (may be what) you saw, O king of the time.
sentences.i: The vizier said to him, “May it be good, what you have seen, O king of the age!”
sentences.n: khayran raʾayta, “good you have seen”, the stock reply to anyone about to tell a dream: a wish that the dream may bode well. malik al-zamān, “king of the age”, the usual courtly address.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ أَيُّهَا الْوَزِيرُ رَأَيْتُ أَنِّي فِي حُفْرَةٍ عَلَى صِفَةِ بِئْرٍ أَسْوَدَ وَكَأَنَّ أَقْوَامًا يُعَذِّبُونَنِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu ayyuhā al-wazīru raʾaytu annī fī ḥufratin ʿalā ṣifati biʾrin aswada wa-ka-anna aqwāman yuʿadhdhibūnanī
sentences.l: And he said to him: O vizier, I saw that I (was) in a pit in the likeness of a well, black, and as-if people were tormenting me.
sentences.i: The king said, “Vizier, I dreamed that I was in a pit like a black well, and it was as though there were people tormenting me.
sentences.n: ʿalā ṣifati, “in the manner of”, like. biʾr, “well”, is feminine, but its adjective here is masculine, aswad rather than sawdāʾ; perhaps the adjective is meant for the pit as a whole. The print writes ka-anna, “as if”, without its hamza (كان), which makes it look like kāna, “was”; the accusative aqwāman shows that ka-anna is meant. aqwām, plural of qawm, “people, folk”.

sentences.t: فَأَرَدْتُ الْقِيَامَ فَلَمَّا نَهَضْتُ وَقَعْتُ عَلَى أَقْدَامِي وَمَا قَدَرْتُ عَلَى الْخُرُوجِ مِنْ تِلْكَ الْحُفْرَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-aradtu al-qiyāma fa-lammā nahaḍtu waqaʿtu ʿalā aqdāmī wa-mā qadartu ʿalā al-khurūji min tilka al-ḥufrati
sentences.l: And I wanted the rising; and when I got-up I fell upon my feet, and I was not able to (do) the getting-out from that pit.
sentences.i: I tried to get up, but when I rose I fell back on my feet, and I could not get out of that pit.
sentences.n: waqaʿtu ʿalā aqdāmī, “I fell upon my feet”: the picture seems to be that he springs up and drops back to where he stood, unable to climb out; the exact sense is not certain. aqdām, “feet”, is a plural used for the pair, as often in later Arabic. qadara ʿalā, “to be able to”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ الْتَفَتُّ فَرَأَيْتُ فِيهَا مِنْطَقَةً مِنْ ذَهَبٍ فَمَدَدْتُ يَدِي لِآخُذَهَا
sentences.tr: thumma iltafattu fa-raʾaytu fīhā minṭaqatan min dhahabin fa-madadtu yadī li-ākhudhahā
sentences.l: Then I turned, and I saw in it a belt of gold, and I stretched-out my hand to take it.
sentences.i: Then I looked round and saw a golden belt lying in it, and I stretched out my hand to take it.
sentences.n: iltafata, “to turn the head, look round”. minṭaqa, “belt, girdle”, from naṭaqa, “to gird”. li-ākhudhahā: li- with the subjunctive, “in order to take it”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَفَعْتُهَا مِنَ الْأَرْضِ رَأَيْتُهَا مِنْطَقَتَيْنِ فَشَدَدْتُ وَسَطِي بِهِمَا فَإِذَا هُمَا قَدْ صَارَتَا مِنْطَقَةً وَاحِدَةً
sentences.tr: fa-lammā rafaʿtuhā mina al-arḍi raʾaytuhā minṭaqatayni fa-shadadtu wasaṭī bihimā fa-idhā humā qad ṣāratā minṭaqatan wāḥidatan
sentences.l: And when I lifted it from the ground, I saw it (to be) two belts; and I bound my middle with them, and behold, they two had become one belt.
sentences.i: When I lifted it from the ground I saw that it was two belts. I girded my waist with them, and suddenly the two had become a single belt.
sentences.n: minṭaqatayni, dual, “two belts”; ṣāratā, the feminine dual of the verb, “the two became”. fa-idhā, “and behold”, marks the sudden turn. The two belts that join into one carry the meaning of the dream, as the vizier will explain.

sentences.t: وَهٰذَا أَيُّهَا الْوَزِيرُ مَنَامِي وَالَّذِي رَأَيْتُهُ فِى الَذِيذِ أَحْلَامِي
sentences.tr: wa-hādhā ayyuhā al-wazīru manāmī wa-alladhī raʾaytuhu fī ladhīdhi aḥlāmī
sentences.l: And this, O vizier, (is) my dream, and that-which I saw in the sweetest of my dreams.
sentences.i: That, vizier, is my dream, what I saw in the sweetest of my dreams.
sentences.n: The print has رابته, a misprint for رايته (raʾaytuhu, “I saw it”), corrected here. The next word is printed الذيذ, which is not a word as it stands: it is read here as ladhīdhi aḥlāmī, “the sweetest of my dreams” (an adjective set before its noun), with a stray alif; it could equally be meant for aladhdhi aḥlāmī, with the same sense. The print's letters are kept. Rhyme: manāmī / aḥlāmī.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْوَزِيرُ دَنْدَانُ اعْلَمْ يَا مَوْلَانَا السُّلْطَانَ أَنَّ رُؤْيَاكَ تَدُلُّ عَلَى أَنَّ لَكَ أَخًا أَوِ ابْنَ أَخٍ أَوِ ابْنَ عَمٍّ أَوْ أَحَدًا يَكُونُ مِنْ أَهْلِكَ مِنْ دَمِكَ وَلَحْمِكَ وَعَلَى كُلِّ حَالٍ هُوَ مِنَ الْعَصَبِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-wazīru Dandānu iʿlam yā mawlānā al-sulṭāna anna ruʾyāka tadullu ʿalā anna laka akhan awi ibna akhin awi ibna ʿammin aw aḥadan yakūnu min ahlika min damika wa-laḥmika wa-ʿalā kulli ḥālin huwa mina al-ʿaṣabi
sentences.l: And the vizier Dandān said to him: Know, O our master the sultan, that your vision points to that you have a brother or a son of a brother or a son of a paternal-uncle, or someone who is of your people, of your blood and your flesh; and in every case he is of the kin-by-the-father.
sentences.i: The vizier Dandān answered him, “Know, our lord sultan, that your dream shows that you have a brother, or a brother's son, or a cousin, or someone of your own family, of your own blood and flesh. In any case, he is of your father's kin.”
sentences.n: The print has روباك, a misprint for رؤياك (ruʾyāka, “your vision”), corrected here. ruʾyā, “a vision in sleep, a dream”. dalla ʿalā, “to point to, indicate”. yā mawlānā al-sulṭāna: the title stands in apposition to the vocative and takes its accusative. al-ʿaṣab, here “the kin through the male line”, the sense of the commoner ʿaṣaba; the same word means “sinews”, which suits the blood and flesh just before. The belts that become one are the kinsmen who will be joined to him.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ الْمَلِكُ هٰذَا الْكَلَامَ نَظَرَ إِلَى كَانَ مَاكَانَ وَنُزْهَةِ الزَّمَانِ وَقَضَى فَكَانَ وَالْوَزِيرِ دَنْدَانَ وَمَنْ مَعَهُمْ مِنَ الْأُسَارَى
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-maliku hādhā al-kalāma naẓara ilā Kāna Mā Kāna wa-Nuzhati al-Zamāni wa-Qaḍā Fakāna wa-al-wazīri Dandāna wa-man maʿahum mina al-usārā
sentences.l: And when the king heard this speech, he looked at Kān Mā Kān and Nuzhat al-Zamān and Qaḍā Fakān and the vizier Dandān, and whoever (was) with them of the captives.
sentences.i: When the king heard these words, he looked at Kān Mā Kān, Nuzhat al-Zamān, Qaḍā Fakān, the vizier Dandān and the other captives with them.
sentences.n: usārā, plural of asīr, “captive”, a by-form of asrā. Dandān takes the diptote ending -a in the genitive (wa-al-wazīri Dandāna).

sentences.t: وَقَالَ فِي نَفْسِهِ إِذَا رَمَيْتُ رِقَابَ هٰؤُلَاءِ انْقَطَعَتْ قُلُوبُ عَسْكَرِهِمْ بِهَلَاكِ أَصْحَابِهِمْ وَرَجَعْتُ إِلَى بِلَادِي عَنْ قَرِيبٍ لِئَلَّا يَخْرُجَ الْمُلْكُ مِنْ يَدِي
sentences.tr: wa-qāla fī nafsihi idhā ramaytu riqāba hāʾulāʾi inqaṭaʿat qulūbu ʿaskarihim bi-halāki aṣḥābihim wa-rajaʿtu ilā bilādī ʿan qarībin li-allā yakhruja al-mulku min yadī
sentences.l: And he said in himself: If I throw-off the necks of these, the hearts of their army will be-cut-off by the perishing of their companions, and I will return to my lands soon, lest the kingship go-out from my hand.
sentences.i: And he said to himself, “If I strike off the heads of these people, their army's heart will break at the death of their comrades, and I can go back to my own country soon, before the kingdom slips out of my hands.”
sentences.n: qāla fī nafsihi, “he said in himself”, thought. ramā al-raqaba, “to throw off the neck”, to behead. inqaṭaʿa al-qalb, “the heart is cut off”, to lose heart, despair. The perfect verbs after idhā carry future sense, “if I strike … their hearts will break … and I will go back”. ʿan qarībin, “before long”. al-mulk, “sovereignty, kingship”, not al-malik, “the king”. li-allā, “so that … not”, lest.

sentences.t: وَلَمَّا صَمَّمَ عَلَى ذٰلِكَ اسْتَدْعَى بِالسَّيَّافِ وَأَمَرَهُ أَنْ يَضْرِبَ رَقَبَةَ كَانَ مَاكَانَ مِنْ وَقْتِهِ وَسَاعَتِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-lammā ṣammama ʿalā dhālika istadʿā bi-al-sayyāfi wa-amarahu an yaḍriba raqabata Kāna Mā Kāna min waqtihi wa-sāʿatihi
sentences.l: And when he had resolved upon that, he called for the swordsman, and commanded him that he strike the neck of Kān Mā Kān from its time and its hour.
sentences.i: When he had made up his mind to it, he summoned the executioner and ordered him to strike off Kān Mā Kān's head then and there.
sentences.n: ṣammama ʿalā, “to be firmly resolved on”. istadʿā bi-, “to call for, summon”: the verb takes bi- of the one sent for, as daʿā bi- does. sayyāf, “swordsman”, the executioner at a king's court. min waqtihi wa-sāʿatihi, “from its time and its hour”: at once, on the spot.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا بِدَايَةِ الْمَلِكِ قَدْ أَقْبَلَتْ فِي تِلْكَ السَّاعَةِ فَقَالَتْ لَهُ أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ عَلَى مَاذَا عَوَّلْتَ
sentences.tr: wa-idhā bi-dāyati al-maliki qad aqbalat fī tilka al-sāʿati fa-qālat lahu ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu ʿalā mādhā ʿawwalta
sentences.l: And behold, the nurse of the king had come-forward in that hour, and she said to him: O king the happy, upon what have you resolved?
sentences.i: Just then the king's old nurse came in and said to him, “Fortunate king, what have you decided to do?”
sentences.n: dāyat al-malik, “the king's nurse”. dāya is the woman who nursed and reared a child, and often stays on as a trusted servant in the household. ʿawwala ʿalā, “to resolve on, settle on”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا عَوَّلْتُ عَلَى قَتْلِ هٰؤُلَاءِ الْأُسَارَى الَّذِينَ فِي قَبْضَتِي وَبَعْدَ ذٰلِكَ أَرْمِي رُؤُسَهُمْ إِلَى أَصْحَابِهِمْ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā ʿawwaltu ʿalā qatli hāʾulāʾi al-usārā alladhīna fī qabḍatī wa-baʿda dhālika armī ruʾūsahum ilā aṣḥābihim
sentences.l: And he said to her: I have resolved on the killing of these captives who (are) in my grip, and after that I throw their heads to their companions.
sentences.i: He said, “I have decided to kill these captives I hold in my hands, and then to throw their heads to their comrades.
sentences.n: qabḍa, “grip, grasp”: fī qabḍatī, “in my power”. ruʾūs, “heads”, is printed with a single wāw (رؤس), a common spelling of ruʾūs.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَحْمِلُ أَنَا وَأَصْحَابِي عَلَيْهِمْ جُمْلَةً وَاحِدَةً فَنَقْتُلُ الَّذِي نَقْتُلُهُ وَنَهْزِمُ الْبَاقِى وَتَكُونُ هٰذِهِ وَقْعَةَ الِانْفِصَالِ وَأَرْجِعُ إِلَى بِلَادِي عَنْ قَرِيبٍ قَبْلَ أَنْ يَحْدُثَ بَعْدَ الْأُمُورِ أُمُورٌ فِي مَمْلَكَتِي
sentences.tr: thumma aḥmilu anā wa-aṣḥābī ʿalayhim jumlatan wāḥidatan fa-naqtulu alladhī naqtuluhu wa-nahzimu al-bāqiya wa-takūnu hādhihi waqʿata al-infiṣāli wa-arjiʿu ilā bilādī ʿan qarībin qabla an yaḥdutha baʿda al-umūri umūrun fī mamlakatī
sentences.l: Then I charge, I and my companions, upon them (in) one body, and we kill whom we kill and rout the remainder; and this will be the battle of the separation, and I return to my lands soon, before there happen, after the affairs, affairs in my kingdom.
sentences.i: Then my men and I will charge them all at once, kill whom we kill and rout the rest. That will be the battle that settles it, and I shall go home soon, before anything more happens in my kingdom on top of all this.”
sentences.n: ḥamala ʿalā, “to bear down on”, to charge. jumlatan wāḥidatan, “as one whole”, all together. fa-naqtulu alladhī naqtuluhu, “we kill whom we kill”: an open-ended phrase, as many as fall to us. waqʿat al-infiṣāl, “the battle of the parting”, the one that decides the war and ends it. baʿda al-umūri umūrun, “after the affairs, affairs”: fresh troubles on top of the present ones. The print writes al-bāqī with a dotless yāʾ (الباقى).

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ مَا سَمِعَتْ مِنْهُ دَايَتُهُ هٰذَا الْكَلَامَ أَقْبَلَتْ عَلَيْهِ وَقَالَتْ لَهُ بِلِسَانِ الْإِفْرَنْجِ كَيْفَ يَطِيبُ عَلَيْكَ أَنْ تَقْتُلَ ابْنَ أَخِيكَ وَأُخْتَكَ وَابْنَةَ أُخْتِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda mā samiʿat minhu dāyatuhu hādhā al-kalāma aqbalat ʿalayhi wa-qālat lahu bi-lisāni al-Ifranji kayfa yaṭību ʿalayka an taqtula ibna akhīka wa-ukhtaka wa-ibnata ukhtika
sentences.l: And at what his nurse heard from him this speech, she came-close to him and said to him in the tongue of the Franks: How is it pleasant to you that you kill the son of your brother, and your sister, and the daughter of your sister?
sentences.i: As soon as his nurse heard him say this, she turned to him and said in the language of the Franks, “How can you bear to kill your brother's son, your sister, and your sister's daughter?”
sentences.n: fa-ʿinda mā, “at the moment that”, as soon as; the print sets ʿinda and mā apart. aqbala ʿalā, “to turn towards someone”. bi-lisāni al-Ifranj, “in the tongue of the Franks”, so that the captives will not understand. ṭāba li-, “to be pleasant to”, is the Classical construction; ṭāba ʿalā is spoken usage. Kān Mā Kān is the son of Rūmzān's half-brother Ḍawʾ al-Makān; Nuzhat al-Zamān is his half-sister, and Qaḍā Fakān her daughter.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ الْمَلِكُ مِنْ دَايَتِهِ هٰذَا الْكَلَامَ اغْتَاظَ غَيْظًا شَدِيدًا وَقَالَ لَهَا يَا مَلْعُونَةُ أَلَمْ تَعْلَمِي أَنَّ أُمِّي قَدْ قُتِلَتْ وَأَنَّ أَبِي قَدْمَاتَ مَسْمُومًا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-maliku min dāyatihi hādhā al-kalāma ightāẓa ghayẓan shadīdan wa-qāla lahā yā malʿūnatu a-lam taʿlamī anna ummī qad qutilat wa-anna abī qad māta masmūman
sentences.l: And when the king heard from his nurse this speech, he raged a raging intense, and said to her: O accursed-one, do you not know that my mother was killed, and that my father died poisoned?
sentences.i: When the king heard these words from his nurse, he flew into a violent rage and said to her, “Curse you, don't you know that my mother was murdered, and that my father died of poison?
sentences.n: ightāẓa ghayẓan shadīdan, a verb with its own noun, “raged with great rage”. a-lam, “did … not?”: the question particle a- with lam. The print runs qad into māta (قدمات). Abrīza was killed long ago by the slave al-Ghaḍbān; King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān was poisoned through Dhāt al-Dawāhī's plotting.

sentences.t: وَأَعْطَيْتِنِي خَرَزَةً وَقُلْتِ لِي إِنَّ هٰذِهِ الْخَرَزَهَ كَانَتْ لِأَبِيكَ فَلِمَ لَاتَصْدُقِينِي فِى الْحَدِيثِ
sentences.tr: wa-aʿṭaytinī kharazatan wa-qulti lī inna hādhihi al-kharazata kānat li-abīka fa-lima lā taṣduqīnī fī al-ḥadīthi
sentences.l: And you gave me a bead and said to me: Truly this bead was your father's. So why do you not speak-true to me in the account?
sentences.i: You gave me a bead and told me it had belonged to my father. So why don't you tell me the truth about it?
sentences.n: kharaza, “bead”, a jewel or amulet bead strung on a cord: this is presumably one of the jewels that King ʿUmar gave Abrīza long before. The print spells it here with hāʾ for tāʾ marbūṭa (الخرزه), a habit of the edition, and runs lā into taṣduqīnī. taṣduqīnī, “you tell me the truth”, lacks the -na of the indicative (Classical taṣduqīnanī), a common Middle Arabic form. fa-lima, “so why?”, li- with mā shortened.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ كُلُّ مَا أَخْبَرْتُكَ بِهِ صِدْقٌ وَلَكِنْ شَأْنِي وَشَأْنُكَ عَجِيبٌ وَأَمْرِي وَأَمْرُكَ غَرِيبٌ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu kullu mā akhbartuka bihi ṣidqun wa-lākin shaʾnī wa-shaʾnuka ʿajībun wa-amrī wa-amruka gharībun
sentences.l: And she said to him: All that I told you of (is) truth, but my case and your case (are) wondrous, and my affair and your affair strange.
sentences.i: She said, “Everything I have told you is true, but my story and yours are a wonder, and our fortunes are strange.
sentences.n: shaʾn and amr, “case, affair”, used in parallel. Rhyme: ʿajīb / gharīb. The print writes shaʾnī and shaʾnuka without hamza (شاني, شانك).

sentences.t: فَإِنَّنِي أَنَا اسْمِي مَرْجَانَةُ وَاسْمُ أُمِّكَ أَبْرِيزَةُ وَكَانَتْ ذَاتَ حُسْنٍ وَجَمَالٍ وَشَجَاعَتُهَا تُضْرَبُ بِهَا الْأَمْثَالُ وَاشْتَهَرَتْ بِالشَّجَاعَةِ بَيْنَ الْأَبْطَالِ
sentences.tr: fa-innanī anā ismī Marjānatu wa-ismu ummika Abrīzatu wa-kānat dhāta ḥusnin wa-jamālin wa-shajāʿatuhā tuḍrabu bihā al-amthālu wa-ishtaharat bi-al-shajāʿati bayna al-abṭāli
sentences.l: For truly I, my name (is) Marjāna, and the name of your mother (is) Abrīza; and she was possessed of beauty and loveliness, and her courage, proverbs were struck by it, and she became-famous for courage among the champions.
sentences.i: I am Marjāna, and your mother's name was Abrīza. She was a woman of great beauty and loveliness; her courage was a byword, and she was famed for it among the champions.
sentences.n: Marjāna was Abrīza's maid in the earlier part of the tale. fa-innanī anā ismī, “for I, I, my name is”: the speaker set first and taken up again by the pronoun. ḍuribat bihi al-amthāl, “proverbs are struck by it”: it became a byword. Rhyme: jamāl / amthāl / abṭāl.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا أَبُوكَ فَإِنَّهُ الْمَلِكُ عُمَرُ بْنُ النُّعْمَانِ صَاحِبُ بَغْدَادَ وَخُرَاسَانَ مِنْ غَيْرِ شَكٍّ وَلَارَيْبٍ وَلَارَجْمِ غَيْبٍ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā abūka fa-innahu al-maliku ʿUmaru ibnu al-Nuʿmāni ṣāḥibu Baghdāda wa-Khurāsāna min ghayri shakkin wa-lā raybin wa-lā rajmi ghaybin
sentences.l: And as for your father, truly he (is) King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, lord of Baghdad and Khurāsān, without doubt and no suspicion and no casting at the unseen.
sentences.i: As for your father, he was King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, lord of Baghdad and Khurāsān, beyond any doubt or question or guesswork.
sentences.n: ammā … fa-, “as for … then”. ṣāḥib, “owner, master”, here “ruler of”. rajm al-ghayb, “stoning the unseen”, a guess in the dark (compare the Qurʾānic rajman bi-al-ghayb, 18:22). The print runs lā into raybin and rajmi (لاريب, لارجم). Rhyme: al-Nuʿmān / Khurāsān; rayb / ghayb.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ قَدْأَرْسَلَ وَلَدَهُ شَرْكَانَ إِلَى بَعْضِ غَزَوَاتِهِ صُحْبَةَ هٰذَا الْوَزِيرِ دَنْدَانَ وَكَانَ مِنْهُمُ الَّذِي قَدْكَانَ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna qad arsala waladahu Sharrukāna ilā baʿḍi ghazawātihi ṣuḥbata hādhā al-wazīri Dandāna wa-kāna minhumu alladhī qad kāna
sentences.l: And he had sent his son Sharrukān to one of his raids in the company of this vizier Dandān, and there was from them that-which had been.
sentences.i: He had sent his son Sharrukān off on one of his campaigns in the company of this vizier Dandān, and what happened to them happened.
sentences.n: kāna qad arsala, “he had sent”, the pluperfect. ghazwa, plural ghazawāt, “raid, campaign”. ṣuḥbata, “in the company of”, used as a preposition, a later usage. wa-kāna minhum alladhī qad kāna, “and there was from them what had been”: a storyteller's shrug that passes over events the listener already knows. The print runs qad into the next word twice here (قدارسل, قدكان).

sentences.t: وَكَانَ أَخُوكَ الْمَلِكُ شَرْكَانُ تَقَدَّمَ عَلَى الْجُيُوشِ وَانْفَرَدَ وَحْدَهُ عَنْ عَسْكَرِهِ فَوَقَعَ عِنْدَ أُمِّكَ الْمَلِكَةِ أَبْرِيزَةَ فِي قَصْرِهَا
sentences.tr: wa-kāna akhūka al-maliku Sharrukānu taqaddama ʿalā al-juyūshi wa-infarada waḥdahu ʿan ʿaskarihi fa-waqaʿa ʿinda ummika al-malikati Abrīzata fī qaṣrihā
sentences.l: And your brother King Sharrukān had gone-ahead of the armies and gone-apart alone from his troops, and he fell-in with your mother Queen Abrīza in her palace.
sentences.i: Your brother, King Sharrukān, had ridden on ahead of the armies and become separated from his troops, and he chanced upon your mother, Queen Abrīza, at her palace.
sentences.n: Sharrukān is Rūmzān's half-brother: both are sons of King ʿUmar. kāna … taqaddama, “had gone ahead”: kāna with a following perfect sets the action back in time. infarada ʿan, “to be cut off from, go off alone”. waqaʿa ʿinda, “to fall in at”, to come upon by chance.

sentences.t: وَنَزَلْنَا وَإِيَّاهَا فِي خَلْوَةٍ لِلصِّرَاعِ فَصَادَفَنَا وَنَحْنُ عَلَى تِلْكَ الْحَالَةِ فَتَصَارَعَ مَعَ أُمِّكَ وَغَلَبَتْهُ لِبَاهِرِ حُسْنِهَا وَشَجَاعَتِهَا
sentences.tr: wa-nazalnā wa-iyyāhā fī khalwatin li-al-ṣirāʿi fa-ṣādafanā wa-naḥnu ʿalā tilka al-ḥālati fa-taṣāraʿa maʿa ummika wa-ghalabathu li-bāhiri ḥusnihā wa-shajāʿatihā
sentences.l: And we had gone-down, and she (with us), into a secluded-place for the wrestling, and he came-upon us while we (were) in that state; and he wrestled with your mother, and she overcame him by the dazzling of her beauty and her courage.
sentences.i: We had gone down with her to a secluded spot to wrestle, and he came upon us while we were at it. He wrestled with your mother, and she overcame him by her dazzling beauty and her courage.
sentences.n: nazalnā wa-iyyāhā, “we went down, and her (with us)”: wa- of accompaniment with the independent object pronoun iyyāhā, a Classical turn. khalwa, “a place of privacy, seclusion”. ṣādafa, “to come upon, find by chance”. li-bāhiri ḥusnihā, “because of the dazzling of her beauty”: bāhir, “dazzling, overpowering”, set before its noun as in laṭīf al-kalām; li- gives the cause.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ اسْتَضَافَتْهُ أُمُّكَ مُدَّةَ خَمْسَةِ أَيَّامٍ فِي قَصْرِهَا
sentences.tr: thumma istaḍāfathu ummuka muddata khamsati ayyāmin fī qaṣrihā
sentences.l: Then your mother hosted him (for) a space of five days in her palace.
sentences.i: Then your mother kept him as her guest for five days in her palace.
sentences.n: istaḍāfa, normally “to ask for hospitality”, here used for its reverse, “to take as a guest, entertain”: a later usage. muddata, “for the space of”, an accusative of time.

sentences.t: فَبَلَغَ أَبُوهَا ذَلِكَ الْخَبَرَ مِنْ أُمِّهِ الْعَجُوزِ شَوَاهِي الْمُلَقَّبَةِ بِذَاتِ الدَّوَاهِي
sentences.tr: fa-balagha abūhā dhālika al-khabara min ummihi al-ʿajūzi Shawāhī al-mulaqqabati bi-Dhāti al-Dawāhī
sentences.l: And her father came-to-know that news from his mother, the old-woman Shawāhī, the one-surnamed Dhāt al-Dawāhī.
sentences.i: Word of this reached her father through his own mother, the old woman Shawāhī, who was called Dhāt al-Dawāhī.
sentences.n: balagha, “to reach”, here with the person as subject and the news as object: “her father reached (learned) that news”. Dhāt al-Dawāhī, “She of the Calamities”, is the nickname of Shawāhī, mother of King Ḥardūb and Abrīza's grandmother; the name rhymes with Shawāhī.

sentences.t: وَكَانَتْ أُمُّكَ قَدْأَسْلَمَتْ عَلَى يَدِ شَرْكَانَ أَخِيكَ فَأَخَذَهَا وَتَوَجَّهَ بِهَا إِلَى مَدِينَةِ بَغْدَادَ سِرًّا
sentences.tr: wa-kānat ummuka qad aslamat ʿalā yadi Sharrukāna akhīka fa-akhadhahā wa-tawajjaha bihā ilā madīnati Baghdāda sirran
sentences.l: And your mother had become-Muslim at the hand of Sharrukān your brother; so he took her and headed with her to the city of Baghdad secretly.
sentences.i: Your mother had embraced Islam at the hands of Sharrukān, your brother, and he took her away with him to the city of Baghdad in secret.
sentences.n: aslama ʿalā yadi fulān, “to become a Muslim at someone's hand”, that is, through him and in his presence. The print runs قد and اسلمت together as one word.

sentences.t: وَكُنْتُ أَنَا وَرَيْحَانَةُ وَعِشْرُونَ جَارِيَةً مَعَهَا وَكُنَّا قَدْ أَسْلَمْنَا كُلُّنَا عَلَى يَدِ الْمَلِكِ شَرْكَانَ
sentences.tr: wa-kuntu anā wa-Rayḥānatu wa-ʿishrūna jāriyatan maʿahā wa-kunnā qad aslamnā kullunā ʿalā yadi al-maliki Sharrukāna
sentences.l: And I was, I and Rayḥāna and twenty slave-girls, with her; and we had become-Muslim, all of us, at the hand of King Sharrukān.
sentences.i: I was with her, I and Rayḥāna and twenty slave-girls, and all of us had become Muslims at the hands of King Sharrukān.
sentences.n: kuntu, “I was”, agrees with the first of its several subjects (anā wa-Rayḥānatu wa-ʿishrūna jāriyatan) instead of taking the plural kunnā, which follows at once in the next clause.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا دَخَلْنَا عَلَى أَبِيكَ الْمَلِكِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ وَرَأَي أُمَّكَ الْمَلِكَةَ أَبْرِيزَةَ وَقَعَ فِي قَلْبِهِ مَحَبَّتُهَا فَدَخَلَ عَلَيْهَا لَيْلَةً وَاخْتَلَى بِهَا فَحَمَلَتْ بِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā dakhalnā ʿalā abīka al-maliki ʿUmara ibni al-Nuʿmāni wa-raʾā ummaka al-malikata Abrīzata waqaʿa fī qalbihi maḥabbatuhā fa-dakhala ʿalayhā laylatan wa-ikhtalā bihā fa-ḥamalat bika
sentences.l: And when we entered upon your father King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, and he saw your mother Queen Abrīza, love-of-her fell into his heart; so he went-in to her one night and was-alone with her, and she conceived with you.
sentences.i: When we came before your father, King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, and he saw your mother, Queen Abrīza, love for her took hold of his heart. One night he went in to her and lay with her alone, and she conceived you.
sentences.n: The print spells raʾā, “he saw”, with hamza but with a dotted yāʾ at the end (رأي); it is read raʾā. waqaʿa … maḥabbatuhā: a masculine verb before a feminine subject, normal when other words come between them. dakhala ʿalā, “to go in to” a woman, and ikhtalā bi-, “to be alone with”, are the usual discreet terms for intercourse. ḥamalat bika, “she became pregnant with you”.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ مَعَ أُمِّكَ ثَلٰثُ خَرَزَاتٍ فَأَعْطَتْهُمْ لِأَبِيكَ فَأَعْطَى خَرَزَةً لِابْنَتِهِ نُزْهَةِ الزَّمَانِ وَأَعْطَى الثَّانِيَةَ لِأَخِيكَ ضَوْءِ الْمَكَانِ وَأَعْطَى الثَّالِثَةَ لِأَخِيكَ الْمَلِكِ شَرْكَانَ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna maʿa ummika thalāthu kharazātin fa-aʿṭathum li-abīka fa-aʿṭā kharazatan li-ibnatihi Nuzhati al-Zamāni wa-aʿṭā al-thāniyata li-akhīka Ḍawʾi al-Makāni wa-aʿṭā al-thālithata li-akhīka al-maliki Sharrukāna
sentences.l: And there were with your mother three beads, and she gave-them to your father; and he gave a bead to his daughter Nuzhat al-Zamān, and gave the second to your brother Ḍawʾ al-Makān, and gave the third to your brother King Sharrukān.
sentences.i: Your mother had three jewelled beads with her, and she gave them to your father. He gave one bead to his daughter Nuzhat al-Zamān, the second to your brother Ḍawʾ al-Makān, and the third to your brother, King Sharrukān.
sentences.n: aʿṭathum, “she gave them”, uses the masculine plural pronoun for the beads, where Classical would say aʿṭathā; and aʿṭā li-, “give to”, replaces the Classical double object. These are the three amulet beads of the earlier nights. The names rhyme: Zamān, Makān, Sharrukān.

sentences.t: فَأَخَذَتْهَا مِنْهُ الْمَلِكَةُ أَبْرِيزَةُ وَحَفِظَتْهَا لَكَ
sentences.tr: fa-akhadhathā minhu al-malikatu Abrīzatu wa-ḥafiẓathā laka
sentences.l: And Queen Abrīza took it from him and kept it for you.
sentences.i: Queen Abrīza took that one back from him and kept it for you.
sentences.n: The pronoun -hā, “it”, is Sharrukān's bead, the third.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا قَرُبَتْ وِلَادَتُهَا اشْتَاقَتْ أُمُّكَ إِلَى أَهْلِهَا وَأَطْلَعَتْنِى عَلَى سِرِّهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā qarubat wilādatuhā ishtāqat ummuka ilā ahlihā wa-aṭlaʿatnī ʿalā sirrihā
sentences.l: And when her giving-birth drew-near, your mother longed for her people and let-me-see into her secret.
sentences.i: As her time drew near, your mother longed for her own people, and she let me into her secret.
sentences.n: aṭlaʿa fulānan ʿalā, “to acquaint someone with, let him see into” a matter.

sentences.t: فَاجْتَمَعَتْ بِعَبْدٍ أَسْوَدَ يُقَالُ لَهُ الْغَضْبَانُ وَأَخْبَرَتْهُ بِالْخَبَرِ سِرًّا وَرَغَّبَتْهُ فِي أَنْ يُسَافِرَ مَعَنَا
sentences.tr: fa-ijtamaʿat bi-ʿabdin aswada yuqālu lahu al-Ghaḍbānu wa-akhbarathu bi-al-khabari sirran wa-raghghabathu fī an yusāfira maʿanā
sentences.l: So she met with a black slave who was called al-Ghaḍbān, and told him the matter secretly, and made-him-desirous of travelling with us.
sentences.i: So she met in private with a black slave called al-Ghaḍbān, told him the whole business in secret, and won him over to travel with us.
sentences.n: ijtamaʿa bi-, “to meet with”: bi- marks the person met. raghghaba fī, “to make someone eager for”, here by promises of reward.

sentences.t: فَأَخَذَنَا الْعَبْدُ وَطَلَعَ بِنَا مِنَ الْمَدِينَةِ وَهَرَبَ بِنَا وَكَانَتْ أُمُّكَ قَدْ قَرُبَتْ وِلَادَتُهَا
sentences.tr: fa-akhadhanā al-ʿabdu wa-ṭalaʿa binā mina al-madīnati wa-haraba binā wa-kānat ummuka qad qarubat wilādatuhā
sentences.l: So the slave took us and went-out with us from the city and fled with us; and your mother, her giving-birth had drawn-near.
sentences.i: The slave took us, led us out of the city and fled with us, and by then your mother was near her time.
sentences.n: The print points this one word, fa-akhadhanā, “and he took us”, to show that -nā is the object “us”, not the subject “we took”. ṭalaʿa bi- and haraba bi-, “to go out with, flee with”: bi- here means taking someone along.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا دَخَلْنَا عَلَى أَوَائِلِ بِلَادِنَا فِي مَكَانٍ مُنْقَطِعٍ أَخَذَ أُمَّكَ الطَّلْقُ بِوِلَادَتِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā dakhalnā ʿalā awāʾili bilādinā fī makānin munqaṭiʿin akhadha ummaka al-ṭalqu bi-wilādatika
sentences.l: And when we came upon the first-parts of our lands, in a cut-off place, the labour-pains took your mother with your birth.
sentences.i: When we reached the borders of our own country, in a lonely place, the pains of labour with you came upon your mother.
sentences.n: awāʾil bilādinā, “the first parts of our land”, its borders. makān munqaṭiʿ, “a cut-off place”, remote and deserted. al-ṭalq is the pain of childbirth; it is the subject, placed after its object ummaka.

sentences.t: فَحَدَّثَ الْعَبْدُ نَفْسَهُ بِالْخَنَا فَأَتَى فَلَمَّا قَرُبَ مِنْهَا رَاوَدَهَا عَنِ الْفَاحِشَةِ فَصَرَخَتْ عَلَيْهِ صَرْخَةً عَظِيمَةً وَانْزَعَجَتْ مِنْهُ فَمِنْ عِظَمِ انْزِعَاجِهَا وَضَعَتْكَ حَالًا
sentences.tr: fa-ḥaddatha al-ʿabdu nafsahu bi-al-khanā fa-atā fa-lammā qaruba minhā rāwadahā ʿani al-fāḥishati fa-ṣarakhat ʿalayhi ṣarkhatan ʿaẓīmatan wa-inzaʿajat minhu fa-min ʿiẓami inziʿājihā waḍaʿatka ḥālan
sentences.l: Then the slave spoke-to his soul of the obscene, and he came; and when he drew-near to her he solicited her to the indecency. And she screamed at him a great scream and was-alarmed by him; and from the greatness of her alarm she bore you at-once.
sentences.i: Then the slave let his mind turn to filth. He came to her, and when he was close he tried to seduce her. She gave a great scream at him and was so terrified that from the sheer fright of it she gave birth to you on the spot.
sentences.n: ḥaddatha nafsahu bi-, “to talk to oneself about”, to toy with the idea of something. al-khanā is obscenity, foul conduct. rāwadahā ʿan al-fāḥisha, “he sought to entice her to lewdness”, is the Qurʾānic phrase for the attempt on Joseph (Sūra 12). ḥālan, “at once, then and there”, is colloquial usage.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ فِي تِلْكَ السَّاعَةِ قَدْ طَلَعَ فِي الْبَرِّمِنْ نَاحِيَةِ بِلَادِنَا غُبَارٌ قَدْ عَلَا وَطَارَ حَتَّى سَدَّ الْأَقْطَارَ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna fī tilka al-sāʿati qad ṭalaʿa fī al-barri min nāḥiyati bilādinā ghubārun qad ʿalā wa-ṭāra ḥattā sadda al-aqṭāra
sentences.l: And at that hour there had risen in the open-country, from the direction of our lands, a dust that had risen-high and flown, until it blocked the horizons.
sentences.i: At that very hour a cloud of dust had risen in the open country, coming from the direction of our land; it climbed and spread until it shut out the horizon on every side.
sentences.n: The print runs البر and من together as one word (البرمن), read al-barri min. The rhyme falls on ṭār / aqṭār. A rising dust cloud in these tales means riders approaching.

sentences.t: فَخَشِيَ الْعَبْدُ عَلَى نَفْسِهِ الْهَلَاكَ فَضَرَبَ الْمَلِكَةَ أَبْرِيزَةَ بِسَيْفِهِ فَقَتَلَهَا مِنْ شِدَّةِ غَيْظِهِ وَرَكِبَ جَوَادَهُ وَتَوَجَّهَ إِلَى حَالِ سَبِيلِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-khashiya al-ʿabdu ʿalā nafsihi al-halāka fa-ḍaraba al-malikata Abrīzata bi-sayfihi fa-qatalahā min shiddati ghayẓihi wa-rakiba jawādahu wa-tawajjaha ilā ḥāli sabīlihi
